title: WHY DID JESUS WARN ABOUT LUKEWARM FAITH?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS WARN ABOUT LUKEWARM FAITH?
The Most Terrifying Warning Jesus Ever Gave Was Not To A Pagan World—It Was To A Church.
By Gospel Warrior
There are few passages in Scripture that make believers uncomfortable as quickly as the letter Jesus sent to the church in Laodicea.
Not because it is difficult to understand.
But because it is impossible to misunderstand.
Jesus did not accuse them of atheism.
He did not accuse them of abandoning church attendance.
He did not accuse them of denying His existence.
He accused them of something far more common.
Something that quietly slips into Christian lives unnoticed.
Something that can sit in church every Sunday.
Something that can quote Bible verses.
Something that can sing worship songs with raised hands.
Something that can wear the label "Christian" while slowly drifting from the heart of Christ.
Lukewarm faith.
And what makes this warning so shocking is that Jesus did not address it to unbelievers.
He addressed it to His own church.
The words still echo across centuries like thunder.

"So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I am about to spit you out of my mouth."
(Revelation 3:16)
Those words should stop every believer in their tracks.
Because Jesus did not say, "I am disappointed."
He did not say, "I am concerned."
He said He was ready to reject what they had become.
Why?
To understand that answer, we must first understand Laodicea itself.
The City Behind The Warning
Laodicea was one of the wealthiest cities in the Roman world.
It was famous for banking.
It was famous for its black wool industry.
It was famous for its medical school and eye salve.
The city was rich.
Self-sufficient.
Successful.
After a devastating earthquake in AD 60, Laodicea rebuilt itself without financial help from Rome.
They proudly declared they needed nothing.
That attitude slowly infected the church.
They believed their material prosperity proved their spiritual health.
Jesus saw something completely different.
The believers thought they were thriving.
Christ saw a spiritual emergency.
Notice His words:

"Because you say, 'I am rich, I have become wealthy, and need nothing,' and you do not know that you are wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked."
(Revelation 3:17)
The tragedy was not merely their condition.
The tragedy was their blindness to their condition.
They were spiritually dying while believing they were spiritually successful.
And that danger has not disappeared.
In many ways, it has become even more common.
The Original Language Behind "Lukewarm"
The Greek word used in Revelation 3:16 is χλιαρός (chliaros).
It literally means tepid.
Neither refreshingly cold.
Nor passionately hot.
Something that has lost its intended usefulness.
Many modern readers assume Jesus preferred people to be spiritually hot rather than cold.
While that is certainly true, the local context adds a deeper layer.
Laodicea had a water problem.
Nearby Hierapolis was known for its hot mineral springs.
Nearby Colossae was known for its cold, refreshing mountain water.
Laodicea received water through aqueduct systems.
By the time it arrived, the water was often lukewarm.
Not healing.
Not refreshing.
Not useful.
The image would have immediately connected with the first readers.
Jesus was not merely condemning temperature.
He was condemning uselessness.
A faith that no longer refreshes.
A faith that no longer heals.
A faith that no longer transforms.
A faith that bears the name of Christ while lacking the life of Christ.
The Most Dangerous Place To Be
Open rebellion is dangerous.
But spiritual complacency may be even more dangerous.
Why?
Because rebels know they are far from God.
Lukewarm people often believe they are close.
The prodigal son knew he was living among pigs.
The Pharisees believed they were righteous while rejecting the Messiah standing in front of them.
One group was lost and knew it.
The other group was lost and did not.
Jesus repeatedly confronted religious people whose external appearance hid internal decay.

"You clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence."
(Matthew 23:25)
Lukewarm faith often specializes in appearances.
It learns Christian language.
It learns Christian culture.
It learns Christian routines.
Yet slowly loses intimacy with Christ Himself.
The Hebrew Concept We Often Miss
Throughout the Old Testament, God repeatedly calls His people to serve Him with their whole heart.
The Hebrew word is לֵבָב (levav).
It refers not merely to emotion but to the inner person—the center of desire, devotion, thought, and will.
When Moses declared:

"You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart..."
(Deuteronomy 6:5)
The command was not partial affection.
It was total surrender.
Lukewarm faith attempts something Scripture never allows.
It tries to divide the heart.
Part for God.
Part for self.
Part for worship.
Part for comfort.
Part for obedience.
Part for compromise.
Yet biblical faith has always demanded the whole heart.
Jesus later echoed this very truth:

"No one can serve two masters."
(Matthew 6:24)
The Slow Drift Nobody Notices
Very few believers wake up one morning determined to become lukewarm.
It happens gradually.
Prayer becomes occasional.
Scripture becomes optional.
Conviction becomes inconvenient.
Repentance becomes rare.
Comfort becomes king.
The drift is subtle.
A little less hunger.
A little less surrender.
A little less awe.
Until eventually faith becomes something we manage instead of something that consumes us.
The terrifying reality is that lukewarm faith often feels normal.
That is why Jesus warned about it.
What Jesus Offered Instead
The Laodicean letter is not merely a warning.
It is also one of the most beautiful invitations in Scripture.
Jesus says:

"Those whom I love, I rebuke and discipline."
(Revelation 3:19)
Notice the reason.
Love.
Not hatred.
Not rejection.
Love.
The warning exists because Christ still desires restoration.
Then comes one of the most famous images in the Bible:

"Behold, I stand at the door and knock."
(Revelation 3:20)
Many people use this verse in evangelism.
Yet in context, Jesus is speaking to a church.
The heartbreaking picture is that Christ stands outside a congregation bearing His own name.
They had religion.
But they had lost fellowship.
They had activity.
But they had lost intimacy.
They had programs.
But they had pushed Jesus to the margins.
Yet He still knocks.
Still calls.
Still invites.
Still offers restoration.
The Aramaic Heart Of The Invitation
Jesus most likely spoke Aramaic during much of His earthly ministry.
The concept reflected throughout His teaching is deeply relational.
God is not merely seeking religious performance.
He is seeking covenant relationship.
This echoes the intimate language Jesus used when addressing God as "Abba."
The term conveys deep familial closeness.
Not casual familiarity.
Not distant ritual.
Relationship.
The opposite of lukewarm faith is not merely religious intensity.
It is renewed intimacy with Christ.
The Mirror We Cannot Avoid
Every generation reads Laodicea and assumes Jesus is speaking to someone else.
Another church.
Another believer.
Another denomination.
Another generation.
Yet Scripture was preserved because God intended every believer to hear it personally.
The question is not whether lukewarm faith exists.
The question is whether traces of it exist within us.
Have we replaced surrender with routine?
Have we replaced worship with performance?
Have we replaced intimacy with information?
Have we become content with knowing about Jesus while spending little time with Jesus?
These questions are uncomfortable.
But they may also be life-saving.
The Hope Hidden Inside The Warning
Jesus never warns without purpose.
Every warning is an invitation.
Every conviction is an act of mercy.
Every exposure is an opportunity for restoration.
The same Savior who warned Laodicea is the same Savior who died for sinners, restores wanderers, forgives failures, heals broken hearts, and welcomes prodigals home.
His warning about lukewarm faith was not meant to drive believers away.
It was meant to wake them up.
Perhaps that is why this message still burns after two thousand years.
Because every believer knows what spiritual drift feels like.
Every believer has experienced seasons of distance.
Every believer understands what it means to need revival again.
And Jesus still stands at the door.
Still knocking.
Still calling.
Still inviting.
The greatest tragedy is not failing.
The greatest tragedy is becoming comfortable without Him.
One day, many will discover they drifted from Christ long before they ever walked away from church.
